p.src: After Jia Yuanchun returned to the palace from her visit to Prospect Garden, she ordered Tanchun to make a fair copy, in proper sequence, of all the inscriptions and poems composed that day. She arranged them herself, assessing their relative merits, and further ordered that they be carved on stone in the garden as an elegant literary memorial for all time. Jia Zheng therefore had skilled and renowned craftsmen selected from various places to dress stones and carve the inscriptions in Prospect Garden, while Jia Zhen supervised the work with Rong and Ping. Since Jia Qiang was already occupied with managing Wenguan and the other twelve actresses, together with their costumes and related affairs, and could not easily spare the time, Jia Zhen also summoned Jia Chang and Jia Ling to oversee the work. One day, after the wax was melted and the vermilion prepared, the work began. But no more need be said of this.

But no more need be said of this.

p.src: Now, the twelve young Buddhist novices from the Temple of the Jade Emperor and the twelve young Taoist novices from the Bodhidharma Convent had been moved out of Prospect Garden, and Jia Zheng was considering sending them to live separately in various temples. As it happened, Madam Zhou, the mother of Jia Qin who lived in the rear street, had been wondering how she might obtain some position, large or small, from Jia Zheng for her son to manage, so that he could make a little money for their expenses. Hearing of this matter at just the right moment, she came by sedan chair to ask Xifeng for help. Since Xifeng had always found her unassuming and free of pretension, she agreed. After considering what to say, she went to Lady Wang and told her, “These young monks and Taoists must on no account be sent elsewhere. If Her Highness should come out again, they will be needed for the ceremonies. If they are dispersed, it will be a great nuisance to gather such people again when they are needed. In my opinion, it would be better to send them all to our family temple, Iron Threshold Temple. We need only appoint someone to take a few taels each month to buy their firewood and rice, and that will settle the matter. Whenever they are wanted, a message can be sent and they can come at once, without the least trouble.” Lady Wang heard her out and consulted Jia Zheng. Jia Zheng smiled when he heard the proposal. “That reminds me,” he said. “We shall do precisely that.” He immediately summoned Jia Lian.

p.src: At that moment Jia Lian was dining with Xifeng. Hearing himself summoned and having no idea why, he put down his meal and started to leave. Xifeng caught hold of him and said with a smile, “Wait a moment and listen to me. If it is about anything else, I shall not interfere; but if it concerns the young monks, you must arrange it as I tell you.” She then carefully instructed him what to say. Jia Lian laughed. “I know nothing about it. If you are so capable, go and tell him yourself.” At this, Xifeng jerked up her head and laid down her chopsticks. Looking at Jia Lian with a smile that was not quite a smile, she said, “Do you mean that, or are you joking?” Jia Lian laughed. “Yun, the son of Fifth Sister-in-law in the west corridor, has come to me two or three times asking for some work to manage. I agreed and told him to wait. Now that a suitable position has finally appeared, you are snatching it away again.” Xifeng smiled. “Do not worry. Her Highness has said that many more pines and cypresses are to be planted in the northeast corner of the garden, as well as flowers and plants beneath the buildings. When that work begins, I guarantee that Yun shall be put in charge of it.” “If that is truly so,” said Jia Lian, “then all is well. Only, last night, when I merely wanted to try a different way, you twisted your hands and feet and would have none of it.” Xifeng gave a snorting laugh, spat playfully at Jia Lian, lowered her head, and resumed her meal.

p.src: Jia Lian went off laughing. When he reached the front and saw Jia Zheng, the matter did indeed concern the young monks. Following Xifeng’s plan, Jia Lian said, “As matters stand, Qin has grown into a very capable young man. We may as well put him in charge of this affair. In any event, he can simply draw the monthly allowance according to the household regulations.” Jia Zheng ordinarily paid little attention to such matters, so when Jia Lian proposed this arrangement, he readily agreed. Jia Lian returned to his room and told Xifeng, who at once sent someone to inform Madam Zhou. Jia Qin then came to see Jia Lian and Xifeng and thanked them profusely. As a further favor, Xifeng persuaded Jia Lian to advance him three months’ allowance. Jia Qin wrote out a receipt, Jia Lian approved and signed the warrant, and the matching tally was immediately sent out. The treasury duly paid out three months’ provisions, two or three hundred gleaming taels of silver. Jia Qin casually picked up one piece and tossed it to the men who had weighed the silver, telling them to buy themselves some tea. He then had his page carry the money home and went to consult his mother. Without delay he hired a large braying donkey and mounted it himself, then hired several carts. At the side gate of the Rongguo Mansion he called out the twenty-four novices, had them board the carts, and proceeded directly to Iron Threshold Temple outside the city. Nothing further occurred at the time.

p.src: Let us now return to Jia Yuanchun. After arranging the poems on Prospect Garden in the palace, she suddenly recalled the garden’s scenery. Now that her visit was over, Jia Zheng would surely keep the place respectfully sealed and allow no one to enter and disturb it. Would it not become desolate? Moreover, there were several sisters at home skilled in composing poetry and prose. Why not order them to live there, so that neither fair maidens should languish nor flowers and willows lose their luster? Then she reflected that Baoyu had grown up among his sisters from early childhood and was unlike other boys. If he alone were not ordered to move in, he might become lonely and unhappy; this would inevitably distress Grandmother Jia and Lady Wang. It would therefore be best to let him live in the garden as well. Having reached this decision, she sent the eunuch Xia Shouzhong to the Rongguo Mansion with an edict: Baochai and the others were to live freely in the garden, which must not be kept closed or placed under restrictions, and Baoyu was to move in with them and continue his studies there.

p.src: After Jia Zheng and Lady Wang received this decree and Xia Shouzhong had departed, they reported it to Grandmother Jia and sent servants into the various quarters to clean and prepare them, hanging curtains and setting up beds and canopies. The others were not greatly stirred by the news, but Baoyu was beside himself with delight when he heard the decree. He was discussing with Grandmother Jia how he wanted this and would arrange that when a maid suddenly came in and said, “Master Jia is calling for Baoyu.” The words struck Baoyu like a thunderbolt. His excitement vanished at once, his face changed color, and he clung to Grandmother Jia, twisting about her like a barley-sugar twist, utterly refusing to go even if it killed him. Grandmother Jia had no choice but to comfort him. “There, my precious, just go. You have me behind you; he will not dare treat you unjustly. Besides, you wrote that excellent composition. Her Highness has probably ordered you to live in the Garden, so he only wishes to give you a few instructions—no more than a warning not to misbehave there. Whatever he says, simply answer him properly and agree.” While comforting him, she summoned two elderly matrons and instructed them, “Take good care of Baoyu on the way, and do not let his father frighten him.” The matrons assented.

p.src: Baoyu had no choice but to go, shuffling along less than three inches at a step until at last he reached the other side. As it happened, Jia Zheng was discussing affairs in Lady Wang’s room. Jinchuan, Caiyun, Caixia, Xiuluan, Xiufeng, and the other maids were all standing beneath the veranda; when they saw Baoyu coming, they covered their mouths and smiled. Jinchuan caught hold of Baoyu and whispered with a smile, “I have just put fragrant rouge on my lips. Would you care to taste it now?” Caiyun pushed Jinchuan aside and laughed. “He is already feeling miserable, and still you tease him. Go in quickly while the master is still in a good humor.” Baoyu could only edge his way through the door. Jia Zheng and Lady Wang were both in the inner room. Concubine Zhao raised the curtain, and Baoyu entered with his body respectfully bowed. Jia Zheng and Lady Wang were seated opposite each other on the kang, talking. A row of chairs stood below, occupied by Yingchun, Tanchun, Xichun, and Jia Huan. When he came in, only Tanchun, Xichun, and Jia Huan rose to their feet.

p.src: Jia Zheng raised his eyes and saw Baoyu standing before him, graceful in bearing and strikingly handsome. He then looked at Jia Huan, whose appearance was mean and whose manners were uncouth; suddenly he thought of Jia Zhu, and then reflected that Baoyu was Lady Wang’s only living son, whom she had always treasured, while his own beard was already turning gray. These thoughts diminished by eight or nine parts out of ten his usual impulse to dislike and punish Baoyu. After a long pause he said, “Her Highness tells me that you amuse yourself outside every day and are growing increasingly idle. You are therefore to be kept under supervision and to read and write in the Garden with your sisters. You must apply yourself diligently to your studies. If you fail again to behave properly and lead a settled life, you had better beware!” Baoyu repeatedly answered, “Yes, sir.” Lady Wang then drew him down to sit beside her. His three younger siblings resumed their seats as well.

p.src: Stroking Baoyu’s neck, Lady Wang asked, “Have you finished all the pills from the other day?” “There is one left,” Baoyu replied. Lady Wang said, “Tomorrow I shall have ten more fetched. Every night before you go to sleep, have Xiren attend you and take one before retiring.” Baoyu said, “Ever since you gave the order, Mother, Xiren remembers every evening and sees that I take it.” Jia Zheng asked, “Who is Xiren?” “A maid,” replied Lady Wang. Jia Zheng said, “A maid may be called any ordinary name. Who was so affected as to give her a name like that?” Seeing Jia Zheng grow displeased, Lady Wang tried to shield Baoyu by saying, “The Old Lady named her.” “How would the Old Lady know such a phrase?” said Jia Zheng. “It must have been Baoyu.” Realizing he could not conceal it, Baoyu rose and replied, “In reading poetry, I once remembered an old poet’s line: ‘The scent of flowers assails one, heralding the warmth of day.’ As this maid’s surname is Hua, I casually gave her that name.” Lady Wang hurriedly said, “Baoyu, go back and change it. And you need not lose your temper over such a trifle, sir.” Jia Zheng said, “There is no real harm in it, so why change it? It merely shows that Baoyu neglects serious pursuits and devotes himself entirely to such florid phrases and amorous verse.” With that, he suddenly roared, “You worthless beast! Get out!” Lady Wang also said quickly, “Go on. The Old Lady may be waiting for you to dine.” Baoyu assented and slowly withdrew. Grinning, he stuck out his tongue at Jinchuan, then sped away like smoke with the two matrons. Just as he reached the passageway entrance, he saw Xiren leaning against the doorway. When she saw him return unharmed, her face broke into a broad smile and she asked, “What did he want you for?” Baoyu told her, “Nothing much. He was only afraid I would make mischief after moving into the Garden, so he gave me a few instructions.” As he spoke, he returned to Grandmother Jia and related the whole affair. Finding Lin Daiyu there, Baoyu asked her, “Where would you like to live?” Lin Daiyu had just been pondering this question. When Baoyu suddenly asked her, she smiled and said, “I have been thinking that the Xiaoxiang Lodge would be best. I love the few stands of bamboo screening its winding balustrade; it seems more secluded than anywhere else.” Baoyu clapped his hands and laughed. “That is exactly what I thought! I wanted you to live there too. I shall live in Happy Red Court, so we shall be close to each other, and both places are peaceful and secluded.”

p.src: While the two were still discussing their plans, a messenger from Jia Zheng came to tell Grandmother Jia, “The twenty-second day of the second month is auspicious; the young masters and young ladies may move in then. Over the next few days, servants will be sent in to assign and prepare the quarters.” Xue Baochai was assigned to Allspice Court; Lin Daiyu to Xiaoxiang Lodge; Jia Yingchun to Brocade Tower; Tanchun to Autumn Freshness Studio; Xichun to Smartweed Breeze Lodge; Li Wan to Paddy-Sweet Cottage; and Baoyu to Happy Red Court. Each residence was provided with two elderly matrons and four maids, in addition to each person’s wet nurse and personal attendants, as well as separate servants responsible for tidying and cleaning. On the twenty-second they all moved in together, and in an instant the Garden bloomed like embroidered ribbons, while willows stirred in the fragrant breeze; it was no longer desolate as before.

p.src: But let us waste no more words on idle matters. Ever since Baoyu had moved into the garden, he had been perfectly content, with nothing further left for his heart to desire. Every day he stayed among his cousins and the maids, now reading or practicing calligraphy, now playing the qin or chess, painting pictures or composing poems; he even joined them in embroidering phoenixes, playing flower-and-grass games, adorning their hair with blossoms, humming softly, singing under their breath, solving word puzzles, and playing guessing games. There was scarcely an amusement they did not try, and he was exceedingly happy. He composed several poems on scenes of the moment. p.src: Plum spirits and bamboo dreams—the third watch has passed; beneath brocade rugs and a sable quilt, sleep still will not come.

u.src: Plum spirits and bamboo dreams—the third watch has passed; beneath brocade rugs and a sable quilt, sleep still will not come.

p.src: Across the courtyard of pine shadows, only cranes are seen; pear blossoms cover the ground, but no oriole is heard.

u.src: Across the courtyard of pine shadows, only cranes are seen; pear blossoms cover the ground, but no oriole is heard.

p.src: In her emerald sleeves the maiden's poetic heart grows cold; in his golden sable the young lord finds the wine too weak.

u.src: In her emerald sleeves the maiden's poetic heart grows cold; in his golden sable the young lord finds the wine too weak.

p.src: Yet happily the maid knows how to assay fine tea: she sweeps up fresh snow and brews it at once.

u.src: Yet happily the maid knows how to assay fine tea: she sweeps up fresh snow and brews it at once.

p.src: Because of these poems, certain snobs of the time, on learning that they had been written by a twelve- or thirteen-year-old young gentleman of the Rong-guo House, copied them out and praised them everywhere. Another set of frivolous young men, enamored of their elegant and voluptuous lines, inscribed them on fans and walls and were forever chanting and admiring them. Consequently, people even came to ask him for poems and calligraphy, to commission paintings, or to request inscriptions. Baoyu too became rather pleased with himself and spent all day attending to such outside commissions.

p.src: Who would have thought that vexation could arise amid such tranquility? One day he suddenly grew restless: nothing seemed right, indoors or out, and wherever he went he remained dejected. Most of the garden's inhabitants were young girls, still in an innocent, unawakened world, artless and spontaneous. They sat or lay down without self-consciousness and laughed without ulterior thought; how could they know what was now troubling Baoyu's heart? Uneasy at heart, Baoyu lost interest in staying in the garden and idled about outside instead, though always in a dazed, distracted state. Seeing him like this, Mingyan tried to think of some way to cheer him up. He racked his brains, but Baoyu had already grown tired of every amusement he could think of. Then he remembered one thing Baoyu had never yet seen. Having made up his mind, he went to a bookseller and bought a great many novels old and new, unofficial lives of Flying Swallow, Hede, Empress Wu Zetian, and Imperial Consort Yang, as well as romantic tales and play scripts, which he brought back to tempt Baoyu into reading. Baoyu had never seen books of this kind before, and the moment he laid eyes on them, he felt as though he had discovered a priceless treasure. Mingyan repeatedly warned him not to take them into the garden. “If anyone finds out, I'll land in such trouble I won't know what to do!” But how could Baoyu bear not to take them into the garden? After much hesitation, he selected several of the more refined and carefully written sets, carried them inside, and hid them above his bed, reading them secretly whenever no one was around. The coarse and overly explicit ones he kept hidden in the outer study.

p.src: One day in the middle ten days of the third month, after breakfast, Baoyu took a copy of The Story of the Western Wing to the bridge by the Qinfang Sluice. He sat on a rock beneath the peach trees, opened the book, and began savoring it carefully from the beginning. Just as he reached the words “fallen blossoms arrayed in ranks,” a gust of wind swept by, blowing more than half the peach blossoms from the branches until they covered his body, his book, and the ground all around him. Baoyu was about to shake them off, but, fearing he might trample them underfoot, he gathered the petals into the fold of his robe, carried them to the pond, and shook them into the water. The petals floated on the surface, drifting gently to and fro, until at last they passed out through the Qinfang Sluice.

p.src: When he returned, he saw that many petals still lay upon the ground. As Baoyu stood there hesitating, he heard someone behind him ask, “What are you doing here?” Baoyu turned and saw that it was Lin Daiyu, carrying a flower hoe over her shoulder, with a flower bag hanging from it and a flower broom in her hand. Baoyu smiled. “Good, good! Come and sweep up these petals and cast them into the water. I have just thrown a good many in there myself.” Lin Daiyu said, “It is not good to throw them into the water. The water here may look clean, but once it flows beyond the garden, people dump all manner of filth and foulness into it, and the flowers will still be defiled. I have a flower grave in that secluded corner. Let us sweep them up, put them into this silk bag, and bury them beneath the earth. In time they will simply become one with the soil. Would that not be cleaner?”

p.src: Baoyu was delighted to hear this and said with a smile, “Let me put down my book, and I will help you gather them.” “What book?” Daiyu asked. Caught by her question, Baoyu hastily tried to hide it and replied, “Oh, nothing but The Doctrine of the Mean and The Great Learning.” Daiyu laughed. “You are trying your tricks on me again. You had better show it to me at once. Do you imagine I do not have plenty of ways to deal with you?” Baoyu said, “Dear cousin, I am not afraid to show it to you. But once you have read it, whatever happens, do not tell anyone else. It truly is a wonderful book! Once you begin reading, you will forget even to eat.” As he spoke, he handed the book to her. Lin Daiyu set down her flower-gathering tools and took the book. She began at the beginning, and the farther she read, the more she loved it. In less time than it took to eat a meal, she had finished all sixteen scenes, finding its language startlingly brilliant and its lingering fragrance still upon her lips. Though she had finished the book, she remained lost in thought, silently reciting its lines to herself.

p.src: Baoyu smiled. “Well, cousin, what do you think? Is it good?” Lin Daiyu smiled. “It is indeed delightful.” Baoyu laughed. “I am the ‘sorrowful, sickly youth,’ and you are the beauty ‘whose charms could topple kingdoms and cities.’” At these words, Lin Daiyu flushed crimson from cheeks to ears. Her two brows, which seemed ever knitted yet not knitted, shot upright; her eyes, which seemed ever open yet not open, glared at him. Anger colored her delicate cheeks and indignation filled her sensitive face as she pointed at Baoyu. “You wretch, what wicked nonsense! You bring me these lewd words and amorous songs, then learn such shameless phrases from them to insult me. I shall tell Uncle and Aunt!” By the time she said the word “insult,” her eyes were already rimmed with red again, and she turned to leave. Baoyu grew alarmed and hurried forward to stop her. “Dear cousin, please forgive me just this once. I truly spoke amiss. If I meant to insult you, may I fall into the pond tomorrow and be swallowed by a mangy old turtle, then turn into a great turtle myself; and when one day you have become a ‘Lady of the First Rank’ and die peacefully of old age, may I spend eternity carrying the memorial tablet upon my back beside your grave.” This made Lin Daiyu burst into a snicker. Rubbing her eyes, she laughed and said, “Even after frightening me with that whole rigmarole, you still keep talking nonsense. ‘Bah! So it is merely a shoot that never flowers—a spearhead of silver-painted pewter!’” Baoyu laughed when he heard this. “And what about what you just said? I shall tell on you too.” Lin Daiyu laughed. “You claim that you can memorize a passage at a glance; am I not allowed to read ten lines at once?”

p.src: Putting away the book, Baoyu laughed. “Come, let us be sensible and bury the flowers. We will say no more about that.” The two of them gathered the fallen petals and had just finished burying them when Xiren appeared. “I searched everywhere and could not find you, only to discover you hiding here. The Elder Master is unwell. All the young ladies have gone to inquire after him, and the Old Lady has sent word that you are to go too. Hurry back and change your clothes.” Hearing this, Baoyu hastily picked up his book, took leave of Daiyu, and returned to his rooms with Xiren to change his clothes. We shall say no more of him for now.

p.src: Daiyu, seeing Baoyu depart and hearing that none of the other girls were in their rooms, felt lonely and dejected. She was about to return to her own room when, just as she reached the corner of the wall surrounding Pear Fragrance Court, she heard the lilting notes of a flute and the melodious sound of singing from within. Lin Daiyu knew at once that the twelve young actresses were rehearsing a play. But as she had never been particularly fond of plays, she paid no attention and continued on her way. By chance, however, two lines drifted clearly to her ears, not a word lost: “So here the brilliant purples and vivid reds have bloomed everywhere, only to be abandoned to ruined wells and crumbling walls.” The words filled Lin Daiyu with tender melancholy. She stopped and listened closely, and then heard: “On such a glorious spring day beneath so fair a sky, in whose courtyard lie these pleasures that delight the heart and eye?” Hearing these two lines, she nodded and sighed to herself, thinking, “So there is fine writing even in plays. What a pity that people know only how to watch a performance and may never appreciate the true savor within these words.” No sooner had she thought this than she regretted letting her mind wander and missing part of the song. When she listened again, she heard: “For you are fair as a blossoming flower, while youth slips by like flowing water...” At these two lines, Lin Daiyu felt her heart tremble and her spirit reel. Then she heard lines such as “You pity yourself alone in your secluded chamber,” which left her still more intoxicated and entranced. Unable to remain standing, she sank down upon a rock from the artificial hill and savored the meaning of those eight words: “Fair as a blossoming flower, while youth slips by like flowing water.” Suddenly she recalled a line she had recently read in an ancient poem: “Flowing water and fading flowers alike are without feeling”; then another from a lyric: “The water flows, the flowers fall, and spring departs—in heaven and on earth”; and also the line she had just read in The Western Chamber: “Flowers fall, the water bears away the red; ten thousand kinds of idle sorrow.” All these lines came back to her at once and gathered together in her mind. As she pondered them carefully, her heart began to ache and her mind grew dazed; tears fell from her eyes before she knew it.
